various optimization strategies and exposure configurations, further validating
the efficacy of the proposed method.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical gas fixed bed. The temperature distribution readings from the MRI scanner were correlated with the temperature of the heating element, providing us with spatial resolution of approximately 1.5 mm and a 0.15 K accuracy. The imaging technique allowed us to observe the development of temperature profiles over time, including the formation and progression of the thermal boundary layer within the fixed bed.  The results obtained through MRI imaging demonstrate its potential as an effective tool for in situ monitoring of temperature distributions in gas-solid fixed bed systems.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG algorithms is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination of the performance of the solvers is carried out in both parallel and serial computing environments. Furthermore, an effective parallelization of the BDDC solver is achieved through a technique called H-BDDC, which involves a relatively small local system being solved centrally. Overall, this research provides a detailed exploration of advanced numerical methods applied to cardiac mechanics problems of increasing complexity.

The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, storyline development, and post-production enhancements to optimize viewing experience. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, and the advantages and limitations of existing approaches within this field, while exploring promising areas for future research and development.

Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense methods based on this phenomenon are considered insecure and can be bypassed to recover the original unprotected model. However, distinguishing between genuine masking and false security becomes challenging. This research proposes two new measures, Fisher Masking and Adversarial Separability, to address this issue. Notably, these criteria can also assess the efficacy of separation methods in adaptive classification contexts. First, we demonstrate the applicability of our proposed Fisher Masking criterion in detecting masking-based defenses, misleading accuracy pruning, and confusing defenses. Secondly, we employ the Adversarial Separability criterion to evaluate the validity of separation methods in masking and confusing attacks. Lastly, we introduce a novel attack, Multi-Model Confusion, which exploits multiple models separated by a method, showing that this approach can be more efficient than the original model in the confusing attack scenario.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the closed-world nature of their training process. In contrast, real-world scenarios are characterized by their open-ended nature. This paper addresses this discrepancy by introducing an open-world uncertainty concept that captures the potential for future, unknown classes. This paper also suggests modifying the energy function to incorporate this uncertainty, thereby enabling more effective confidence calibration. Rather than relying solely on classification scores or explicit margin terms, this paper demonstrates that energy functions already factor in open-world uncertainty. Moreover, they are sensitive to the number of classes. As such, this paper proposes a novel, highly efficient method for confidence calibration based on re-weighting the squared margin term in the energy function. Moreover, this paper shows that standard confidence calibration techniques are ineffective for enhancing the reliability of 'tail class' predictions - those with lower occurrence frequencies. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new strategy that calibrates predictions for 'head classes' only, resulting in a net improvement in overall performance. The efficacy of this method is validated through experiments on multiple datasets, including MNIST, EMNIST, and a real-world traffic light recognition scenario.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, and decouples process data from the process model through a separation of concerns. We compare this approach to traditional method, and demonstrate its advantages through an experimental analysis. Additionally, we outline two process data enhancement options to improve the underlying processes identified.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a resolution-challenging event. Through type-II SPDC with specific spectral and temporal properties, we demonstrate that entanglement between the photons enables super-resolution enhancement, allowing for improved resolution of the disintegrated photon by measuring the mode spectrum of its partner photon.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators compete for a single prey, feeding at different rates. The model is divided into two distinct timescales: a short timescale, characterized by rapid predation from the second species, and a longer timescale, marked by the effects of the first species. The research reveals that the accumulated effects of the second species' predation can trigger population control and accelerate the development of the first species, thereby enhancing population stability. A detailed exploration of the population's behavior near the switching point is achieved through the analysis of a limiting slow-fast vector field, while experiencing slowness and blowing-up singularities. A specific control strategy is also proposed to efficiently induce a population shift using periodic applications of external controls, whose cost and timing of implementation are optimized to do so at a minimal cost.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.3}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.3}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Additionally, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, as well as an efficient technique for quickly evaluating fence impact during counter example generation. As for the underlying coherence models, our method is fence-coherent, which means it can produce optimal fence sets that allow programs to behave correctly. We apply this technique to a diverse set of benchmarks, which span basic data processing tasks, hardware bugs, and concurrent algorithms, which have been adapted to function with the mentioned types of coherence models.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ or its increments exceeds $2H$, then the density is in $L^{p}$ with $p < 2H/\text{dim}_{\mathcal{H}}(f)$ or $2H/\text{dim}_{\mathcal{H}}(f')$ respectively, making the image $(B^{H}+f)$ have positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable.

X-ray images of COVID-19 patients often mask key indicators of the disease, such as consolidation, which can make predicting ICU admissions difficult. To address this challenge, researchers analyzed a dataset consisting of 1433 images, each paired with metadata detailing the patients' outcomes. They employed an LSTM network to extract relevant features from the images, combining them with clinical data to forecast ICU admission with an accuracy of 74%. The LSTM also identified potential visual features associated with severe disease severity, which they visually validated. Furthermore, the researchers used Gaussian Process Classification to build a simple model that predicted ICU admission based on specific image characteristics, achieving a 71% accuracy. These findings highlight the utility of deep neural networks not only in predicting severe disease severity but also in uncovering subtle indicators of severe infections hidden within medical imaging.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. To achieve this, a Balanced Negative Proposal Attention (BNPA) module is designed to weigh the contribution of each sub-class, determining the sampling priority of relationships. Our method demonstrates a notable decrease in false positives and a substantial performance boost over the current state-of-the-art models on two standard datasets, CO-VR and Flickr-VR.

This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that can handle
both bright and dimly lit conditions under a single framework, also effective
with scarce data, utilizing a single network architecture. To address the
challenge of recognizing actions in low-light environments, we used pre-trained
video representations in bright conditions that were captured without modifications
to the input, and then combined them with frames captured in low-light conditions
which were processed through a random selection of delta transformation matrices.
To further improve the efficiency of training, we implemented a representation
learning loss that utilized a pre-computed similarity matrix from the training
data to guide the model. Our method achieved superior action recognition results
in low-light conditions and comparable performance in well-lit environments,
and also performed well with scarce data, and resulted in enhanced efficiency
during training.

This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This discovery reveals a massive, compact quiescent galaxy core surrounded by a nearby protocluster core galaxy. Additional transients detected in an ultra-diffuse external disk of one of these galaxies were found to have an estimated mass of $10^6\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. When observed at a later date, an extremely dense and massive disk was found to exhibit an active nuclear region, indicating that these transients were likely caused by a single galaxy merger. Furthermore, this evidence suggests that many high-z galaxy mergers may occur without being directly detected, playing a significant role in driving early galaxy evolution. Additionally, this observation was made possible within the context of a massive galaxy group environment, suggesting that such mergers may be more common in dense environments than in the field fields. Additionally, we propose that tidal interactions with nearby galaxies may result in tidal disturbances in external disks of galaxies, encouraging further exploration of tidal interactions as a potential trigger for starbursts in galaxy disks.

We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01741. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise estimates for the CP-violating phase in neutrino mixing and a plausible scale at which flavour symmetries might break for both quarks and leptons. The outcomes of our analysis are again compared with previous findings and current experimental data.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero.

Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's current understanding. With these tools, we evaluate several cryptographic actions, such as those involving full disk decryption, and propose a method that limits, to an extent, the exploitable evidence the government acquires following the compelled decryption of data.

We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new approximation algorithm is presented for general-valued CSPs on classes that have limited connectivity. The proposed method achieves an $O(\lambda^{*})$-approximation, further enabling a simple PTAS on strictly locally finite classes that have limited connectivity.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations.

Recent analyses of lepton flavor universality (LFU) violating decays have suggested that new physics beyond the Standard Model might exist, potentially influencing multiple areas. To gain insights into the nature of this possible new particle, we explore its impact on the decay $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ within a theory where a heavy $U_1$ gauge boson mediates interactions between leptons and quarks. By leveraging low-energy hadronic parameters and $B \to C$ form factors, we derive a set of inequalities that a new physics contribution must satisfy, based on current $B \to C$ data and measurements of $\Lambda_b \to p X_C$. Our findings reveal that the $U_1$ leptoquark model allows for a significant degree of freedom in determining the hadronic form factors $f_+(q^2)$, $f_2(q^2)$, and $f_3(q^2)$, which in turn significantly affects predictions for the branching ratio and kinematic distributions of the decay $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$. Notably, we observe that the magnitude of the new physics contribution is constrained to a maximum of two orders of magnitude by $B \to C$ data, whereas scenarios with larger contributions are incompatible with measurements of $\Lambda_b \to p X_C$. Additionally, we investigate how the leptoquark coupling's effect on the hadronic system influences the

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines in scenarios with limited labeled examples and vast unlabeled datasets, which are common characteristics of real-world scenarios. Cluster-based methods have also been applied to reduce the need for labels, but they often fail to account for both text and audio modalities, as well as cross-modal inconsistencies that are crucial for detecting false news. To address these challenges, we introduce a meta-learning approach that automatically discovers multiple cross-modal clusters for news classification without any labels, and presents a Multimodal Fake News detection via Emergent Clusters model, enhanced with a neural process architecture for efficient encoding of coupled multi-modal inputs, which enables us to achieve state-of-the-art results on the recent ANRely dataset.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time.

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific types of algebras and by identifying additional constraints for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research greatly expands our current understanding of set-theoretic solutions and their quantum equivalents, revealing new general patterns in the field.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach is constrained by lack of vector control and high sensitivity to donor placement angles affects its examination.
In this work, we report that by arranging two electron-doped silicon atoms in adjacent locations, we can induce a high sensitivity to valley interference, as predicted in theoretical models, and achieve an exchange interaction of 2.4 MHz through geometric control of donor positions, which rivals the computational demands of many-body systems with precise control over spatial configuration exhibited in these two-body systems.
Our experimental method of creating this sensitive quantum state does not rely on random donor placement and can access computational capacities of silicon-based processors that are otherwise intractable.
The achieved exchange interaction is sufficient for coherent manipulation and can contribute to the development of quantum communication protocols that leverage silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to universal principles that can be effectively captured by analyzing their underlying structure and dynamic behavior. However, simply applying machine learning models, such as graph-based models, to predict system outcomes does not guarantee an accurate decomposition of these models into distinct components representing structure and dynamics. In this study, we investigate whether it's feasible to separately model the structural and dynamic aspects of complex systems with an interactive, graph-based approach. We first examine graph attention networks, a prominent machine learning method, to explicitly decouple dynamics from structure. Our analysis reveals that attention mechanisms conflate these aspects. Next, we evaluate alternative ways to assign graph node weights, exploring their statistical properties. By dissecting the graph attention mechanism, we gain a clearer understanding of its effects. Ultimately, our research provides explicit, interpretable models for predicting system behavior. Not only do these models outperform existing graph-based methods in predicting time series outcomes, but they also offer explicit assignments of node importance. Additionally, we establish a theoretical connection between graph attention networks and linear regression.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

Strong quantum nonlocality, a local hidden variable theory's inconclusive characterization, has been limited to certain multi-dimensional systems lacking a universal proof. We characterize unextendible product bases in heterogeneous systems and identify the locally hidden variable-characterizable measureability as an attribute of such bases, characterized by local hidden unitarity. The characterizations of some complex, high-dimensional systems are impossible under local hidden variable theories. The characterizations of other systems necessitate a global measurement. The localization difficulty, characterizing a system, is also defined and can be characterizable by a product measurement. Our research expands local characterization studies of quantum entanglement, providing a thorough understanding of local hidden variable theories.

The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the algorithm reaches a state of safety, the subsequent phase of achieving absolute accuracy is addressed. The method is also compared to alternative algorithms in terms of convergence speed and reduction of undesirable movements.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can match against substructures of larger graphs, significantly speeding up the matching process. In order to maximize the runtime advantages of rooted rules, the recent GP 2 compiler has been completely rewritten in Java using the Jazz framework for graph modification, resulting in faster compilation times along with improved maintenance ease.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional spaces is a significant challenge, for which feature extraction is a vital solution. Dimensionality reduction techniques, including feature extraction and selection, are critical components in developing effective classification models for diverse applications, including speech and image recognition. The success of these methods is heavily dependent on the quality and relevance of the extracted features, which is where our proposed contrastive learning-based feature extraction framework excels. Our approach is designed to be versatile, enabling it to be adapted to any classification problem, and is centered on creating optimal features that convey maximal useful information while minimizing redundancy, as determined by reference information. The quality of the features is assessed through a distance metric, and features are ranked by a score that is essential for feature selection. The contrastive learning process is driven by minimizing the distance between feature representations and reference information, which can be actual data, mean vectors, or random samples, and is formulated as an optimization problem that is efficiently solved using proximal gradient descent. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a range of experiments, including speech and image classification, in which it outperformed or matched the results of 10 different baseline methods, yielding a significant improvement in accuracy compared to the best-performing baseline.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits and nonnormalization conditions, as well as fractional diffusion equations with different boundary treatments. These analyses contribute to the understanding of nonlocal terms in mathematical models and the convergence properties of their sequence models under specific conditions.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as observed through [O III], as well as an association between highly luminous infrared sources and blue shifts in H$\alpha$. Furthermore, our analysis revealed an overlap between areas of active nuclear activity and [O III] gas outflows in 5 out of 6 instances where such comparison was possible. These observations support the hypothesis that the interaction of stars with the outflow of gas can influence

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. This study investigates a two-fluid model in which the updraft and downdraft velocities are permitted to vary independently. We evaluate three approaches to generating thermal and moisture fluxes between the two fluids: (i) exchanging the excess of one fluid to the other, (ii) applying both EBPF equations independently, and (iii) adopting a blend of the above methods. The performance of these approaches is assessed through comparison with direct numerical simulation results for a Rayleigh-Benard convection system, typically features used in parameterisation testing. We find that independently applying the Entrainment and Budget Preservation Principles is generally most effective for moisture convection, although exchanging the excess is often slightly more accurate for temperature convection. Exchange schemes tend to outperform the other methods in terms of solving global balance equations.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced into the CMS. By integrating new components like the pixel pilot blades while recording data during various tests and collisions, the detection system was enhanced, improving hit cluster resolution and restoring initial performance levels. This involved developing algorithms to interpret and visualize the complex 5-dimensional hole patterns. This study describes the reconstruction process of the pixel pilot detector in its upgraded state and presents visualization results following application of a new reconstruction algorithm.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter datasets
from diverse sources to evaluate and contrast the performance of various sentiment classification
methods. We examined three prominent pretrained language models including BERT, RoBERTa, and
Multilingual BERT, along with seven distinct classifying them using sequential neural network
models. We also developed and utilized three novel sequential neural network models, namely
SBERT, Transformer, and Attention, in addition to four conventional sentiment classification
algorithms. We concluded the experiment by comparing all models' performance, with the
best result achieved using the Multilingual BERT and our proposed Attention Sequential Neural
Network model.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal behavior of black hole entropy and internal energy in relation to the T-S and T-V diagrams, respectively. Additionally, we explore the thermal properties of the Hawking radiation emitted by this black hole, finding that both the entropy and average photon energy vary with temperature in a non-monotonic manner.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary dependence rests on track
info extracted from video metadata, such as head and body movement data.
However, this information is often missing or inaccurate and useless in many
tourism video scenarios. Neglecting content info present in the video subtitle
can also result in poor performance in this context. This study proposes a
novel, accurate and practical framework that utilizes the rich information
hidden in the video subtitle to successfully predict a viewer's viewport. The
proposed framework initially decodes the implicit information in the video
subtitle to form a logical description of the scene. It then applies a deep
learning-based method to track changes in the viewer's mindset. The proposed
framework was thoroughly tested with real-world data and showed a significant
improvement of 14.3% overall accuracy and 16.7% better head direction accuracy
in comparison to existing methods.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling complex systems, especially in representing time evolution and equilibrium states in quantum many-body systems. However, a fundamental issue with these methods lies in their restriction to a specific type of state decomposition, which may not be optimal for certain applications and could result in misleadingly efficient representations. As a result, researchers have often accepted the limitations of these methods without critically examining their validity. As the focus has increasingly shifted towards time scales and thermal densities comparable to the system's typical interaction strength, some tensor network approaches have even been applied to a broader spectrum of scenarios. As such, there is a pressing need to experimentally verify whether these methods effectively capture the inherent characteristics of thermal states and time-evolving systems across a broader spectrum of scenarios. Through the development of local algorithms, we can compare their产生的 results with those of sophisticated tensor methods, thereby revealing whether they accurately represent the system's behavior or merely coincidentally efficient representations.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to explore the impact of scaling on decoupling phenomena. Specifically, our work illustrates that multiple, sometimes conflicting, approximation techniques for a given surface can all be useful for developing a surface-specific decoupling strategy. For instance, our study develops a uniform polynomial surface decoupling inequality for a two-piece surface consisting of two distinct quadratic components with different centers but aligned open convexity directions. We also develop new applications for our efficient approximation-based strategy, including improvements to the efficiency of a two-dimensional surface approximation and initiation of analogous investigations for similar surfaces.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete.
