To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on pre-determined probabilities. These estimates enable the establishment of explicit, readable connections between sentences for humans. Surprisingly, available datasets for classifier-predicted indicator tasks are scarce, likely due to the manual collection process. To address this limitation, we developed an entirely novel, exogenous method for generating high-quality artificial datasets for this task. This method involves tweaking baseline representations of sentences that contain implicit indicators by incorporating made-up discourse indicators explicitly. These generated examples are then used to train a model to infer the appropriate discourse indicators between sentences. Experimental results show that models trained with our method achieve high accuracy in predicting discourse indicators, surpassing the best existing baseline approaches. Additionally, the model achieves excellent human eval scores of 74.1 F1, demonstrating the efficacy of our method for generating high-quality artificial datasets for this task. Furthermore, the model exhibits generalization capabilities, as it excels in predicting discourse indicators between human-written sentences from existing datasets. These findings highlight the potential of automated semantic annotation techniques in enhancing the readability of extensively annotated texts.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model on the triangular lattice, where the SU(3) representation was placed on each site, analogous to the familiar case of using fundamental representations. They found an extensive, degenerate set of classical ground states in certain, larger SU(3) representations than the fundamental one. A key finding was the discovery of long-range magnetic order from a spin liquid state, characterized by competing Néel and stripe ordering tendencies. A detailed, "sigma-model" analysis was performed near the first critical, large- $D$ threshold, where a transition between a spin liquid and longitudinal order states occurs. A key feature was the emergence of effective, low-energy representations through the combination of adjacent, fundamental representations, akin to a Heisenberg-like mechanism. A model was developed to explain the critical, large- $D$ behavior, revealing a divergent, effective ferromagnetic exchange interaction resulting from the competition between various mechanisms. A consequence of this is that the spin liquid state exhibits instability toward ferromagnetic ordering.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze the Hessian of f at matrix variables, rank-deficient matrix variables, and Burer-Monteiro factorizations, and provide an original third-term characterization. We believe this study is beneficial due to its innovative integration of the global geometry of f, a quotient geometry, and factorizations, as well as providing precise geodesic Hessian characterizations. These contributions may be of interest to the optimization community due to their in-depth exploration of the geometry of convex and nonconvex objectives, subject to fixed-rank constraints.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$.

High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on these particles' parameter space. To overcome this limitation, a new study explores how the presence of cosmic strings could lower the threshold for detecting these particles by a significant margin. In the presence of cosmic strings, particles with masses up to 10^15 GeV could potentially exist, under the condition that the decay products of these particles contribute a minimal fraction to the overall energy density of the universe. Additionally, the study introduces a new, more sensitive constraint on these particles' parameters derived from the observed power spectrum of gravitational waves produced by cosmic strings.

Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its speed mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method revealed that "social" learning algorithms exhibited greater pay-off stability than their "individual" counterparts. Ultimately, our findings indicate that observing and learning from peer actions is essential for achieving a Nash Equilibrium.

The growing threat landscape in cybersecurity demands increased vigilance, 
wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, anomaly detection and threat assessment become 
more feasible, along with other security operations. Nevertheless, 
traditional methods of enriching ontologies based on natural language 
processing and machine learning are hampered by issues in extracting contextual 
conceptual relationships from text. Therefore, sequential Deep Learning models 
capable of navigating through the semantic structures in language and pinpointing 
embedded security vulnerabilities are needed. Our approach incorporates a 
Bidirectional LSTM model, pre-trained on extensive linguistic data, along with 
a Universal Sentence Encoder to enhance the ISO 27001-compliant security 
ontology. By utilizing a high-performance computing platform to analyze vast 
corpora, we have achieved over 80% accuracy in validating the model's 
robustness and capacity for identifying unseen concepts within the ontology 
and web page instances.

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. These findings are supported by theoretical derivation using the stochastic Landau-Ginzburg equation.

The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the spread of the disease. Through an analysis of 48 experimental scenarios, we determined that larger droplets settle more quickly than smaller ones due to gravity, reducing the distance they travel. Conversely, air currents can carry fine droplets for extended periods and long distances. Notably, higher ambient temperatures accelerate the evaporation of droplets, increasing the distance mid-size droplets can travel before settling or disappearing. Consequently, weather patterns significantly impact the spread of viruses and must be considered alongside other factors such as face mask usage, social distancing, and surface disinfection.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also from limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are fully tested against problems including regression problems, part of IPFA 2020 workshop, the proposed framework introduces a comprehensive framework for modeling and solving problems with uncertainty including scientific machine learning applications. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, a diverse range of methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring in both infinite-dimensional functions and solutions.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.
Using an exact partition function, we analyze a unitary matrix model based on a single plaquette configuration at a finite $N$ for both the SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases.

The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a low-resource Dutch-Polinish name entity recognizer demonstrates a remarkable 23.4% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art method.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality categories based on nuclear neutron coverage. 
Comparisons between data and theoretical models including thermal models, 
hydrodynamics and relativistic transport models demonstrate that the thermal model 
can accurately predict Xe-Xe collision data with a model-derived composite model 
producing an improved fit to data. 
The Xe-Xe collision model's simulated particle production is also found to 
align with experimental observations. 
From pion, kaon and proton ratios, reconstructed $\phi$ mesons from decays 
into $K^+K^-$ and $K^-K^+$ exhibit mass distributions centered around 1.010 GeV/$c^2$ 
with a peak width of 0.051 GeV/$c^2$, again showing agreement between data and 
model predictions.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset, a collection of conversational exchanges, is widely utilized for assessing the performance of dialogue state tracking models. However, the inclusion of incorrect labels and assumptions in the original annotations has limited the reliability of this dataset. Although the recent release of the MultiWOZ 2.1 dataset claims to offer corrected labels based on the source data, the consistency checks employed in the process are not entirely flawless. The proposed data cleaning framework, named ASSIST, utilizes a multi-agent system to effectively address label noise in conversational datasets by combining consistency checks with specialized modules that leverage domain knowledge and conversational context. The results indicate that ASSIST is capable of efficiently correcting the quality of annotated conversational labels, surpassing the previous standard set by MultiWOZ 2.1 datasets. Moreover, when used in conjunction with leading dialogue state tracking models, the datasets refined by ASSIST have also yielded notable improvements in model evaluation scores.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST.

We are studying a critical boundary that involves breaking down real polynomials into the sum of squares of other real polynomials, specifically those that don't equal zero. This specific boundary overlaps with another critical boundary that involves nonnegative polynomials and is characterized by polynomials that become zero at at least one point. Our focus lies on distinguishing the elements of a separate category in this critical boundary, specifically those polynomials that are positive everywhere even if some elements within it are nonstrictly positive. Unfortunately, determining whether a given polynomial belongs to this category appears to be an insoluble problem. Interestingly, we have found that whether a given polynomial is positive everywhere can depend on an infinite number of parameters, something that doesn't happen with elements of another category that involve the sum of squares of other polynomials. Another notable difference with elements of this category is that they typically occur in very rare, very small dimensions within the overall polynomial space. Overall, we have found that there are some interesting ways in which polynomials that are positive everywhere differ from those that are nonstrictly positive, including whether they can be written as the product of other polynomials. These elements are in contrast to analogous properties that are common with those elements of the boundary cone that are SOS-nonstrictly positive.

In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from extra neutrino states. We focus on experimentally relevant scenarios, such as high energy experiments involving neutrinos. We discovered that, despite certain limitations, a wide range of non-unitarity values may be achieved. However, more subtle experiments may be required to fully understand the nature of neutrino matter. We also found that the yet-to-be-built FASER$\nu$ experiment may be able to provide a very precise understanding of the nature of neutrino matter.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an extension to handle intersection, complement, and infinite character sets, utilizing coinduction to prove correctness and efficiency, and finally, the development of a working implementation and performance validation through comparative experiments.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been extensively researched. These models combine the strengths of pure monocular SLAM and inertial odometry, offering the best of both worlds. To maximize performance, compact model complexity, and real-time execution are the primary considerations for VIO development. In monocular SLAM, extracting informative features from raw video is a complex task, and to mitigate this, deep learning-based feature extraction methods have been introduced, delivering comparable or better performance than traditional algorithms. However, few research efforts focus on enhancing the efficiency of front-end VIO algorithms using learned feature extraction. To tackle this challenge, a novel approach called External Memory Attention (EMA) is presented as an effective and efficient framework for monocular VIO, consisting of two main components: an (EMA) module and compact state estimator. Specifically, the EMA module integrates dynamic memory management and self-attention mechanisms to efficiently match informative keypoints from raw video streams, whereas the state estimator module leverages the extracted features and inertial data for simultaneous localization and mapping. As a result, the proposed EMA-VIO algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance on several challenging public datasets, while also offering an open-source codebase for future research into memory attention mechanisms and efficient navigation systems.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where magnetic field data is not available. A non-iterative data completion approach is proposed, utilizing the quasi-reversibility method. Stability results, specifically an exponential loss property and smooth solution behavior, are proven. A convergence result for a time-discretized formulation is established. Two numerical schemes are presented and their outcomes demonstrate good performance in recovering missing data.

This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models.

Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as spatial metrics. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of grid cell research over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' metrics functionality, grid cell's sensitivity to various stimuli including humans, and potential underlying mechanisms including grid cells' priority given to visual cues versus olfactory sensory inputs, as well as oscillatory neural activity.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes an  order-of-magnitude change,  going from high speeds in its early stages to solar-like speeds in its later stages.  As solar-type stars spin slower, the impact of anti-solar differential rotation on magnetic cycle generation in them becomes increasingly significant.  Anti-solar differential rotation,   characterized by decreasing polarity-based spectrum speeds,  has been observed in some active regions of the Sun and could potentially drive magnetic cycles in slower-rotating stars.  This study has run magnetic cycle simulations,  utilizing the Babcock-Leighton model,  to investigate the influence of anti-solar differential rotation on magnetic cycle generation across the full lifespan of a solar-type star.  It was discovered that stars with moderate to high rotation speeds and anti-solar differential rotation could sustain activity cycles even as they entered their dormant phases.  However,  in low-rotation-speed stars,  the nature of activity cycles changed,  with some producing activity instead of spots.  These outcomes suggest that activity cycles are possible in slower-rotating stars,  but their durations and outcomes depend on the specific differential rotation patterns they exhibit.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions.

A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of null directions.  Our work provides insights into how this condition applies to quenching processes within holographic models, specifically two-field, non-degenerate quenching scenarios that occur after the collision of two waves with varying energy densities. By formulating an approximate time-series for the entanglement entropy of a spatial region, we find the change in entropy is most significant in the short-term and follows an universal, conformal scaling pattern in the long-term. Additionally, we observe that the rate of entanglement growth has a lower limit determined by the more energetic side and find evidence of a dual dynamics arising from the less and more energetic modes, respectively. These findings are supported by calculations and have implications for understanding the quantum thermodynamics of null directions in the holographic model.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to calculate the exact minimal time for a set of states and, consequently, for all possible time-independent Hamiltonians. For non-unitary dynamics caused by a single decoherence mechanism, we establish the general formula for the exact minimal time. Additionally, we demonstrate that, in the context of decoherence, there exists a crucial relationship (involving ratios) between two asymmetry measures that, when met, allows us to express the minimal time as a function of the smallest relevant decoherence rate.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that it varies significantly from the properties of an oxidized aluminum film. Comparison with density functional theory simulations indicates an carrier concentration in silicon of $10^{19}~\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$. This concentration is attainable through ion implantation used in semiconductor manufacturing. We posit that near-field terahertz spectroscopy is a valuable tool for non-destructive characterization of chip areas relevant to integrated circuit fabrication. With this technology, we can optimize chip design and reduce decoherence in quantum processors.

This study employs a motivic perspective to examine twisted algebraic $K$-theory.
For a variety over a zero-characteristic field and an Azumaya algebra over that
variety, we develop the $\mathcal{A}$-twisted motivic spectral sequence.
By determining the motivic twisted algebraic $K$-theory spectrum as a twisted form
of motivic cohomology, our work expands upon earlier results by Kahn-Levine where the
algebra is derived from a base field.
Our methods utilize a combination of slice filtration and birational geometry to achieve this,
resulting in a representability theorem that expresses twisted $K$-theory space as
an extension of twisted Grassmannian by the twisted integers sheaf.
Resulting corollary, for fields that are not of characteristic one, is a new result,
demonstrating equivalence between twisted $K$-theory and twisted Hodge-theory.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future.

Investigating the chemistry occurring on charged droplets offers valuable insights into enhancing industrial chemical production methods, a phenomenon common in nature. To address this, researchers have developed a novel method using reaction nanoscopy on charged propanediol nanodroplets. By leveraging ultrashort laser pulses, they have established the capability to monitor the droplet's average size, charge distribution, and surrounding near-field. Furthermore, they have demonstrated the sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing two types of propanediol isomers, revealing that certain conditions produce a significantly increased yield of methyl ions. Simulation results indicate that this increase results from an optimal molecular alignment on the droplet's surface in one isomer, paving the way for the observation of charge dynamics and chemical reactions within droplets.

Recent breakthroughs in numerical computation, driven by GPU and TPU advancements, have significantly scaled tensor network algorithms for complex quantum simulation and machine learning applications. The quantum-inspired nature of these algorithms makes them mappable to parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), which can be solved using quantum hardware. Combining quantum processors with high-performance computing (CPU/GPU) systems could leverage the best of both technologies. In this context, a novel approach is proposed where the quantum part of a tensor network calculation is reduced to matrix operations, leaving only the TMTP state construction as a quantum subroutine. By decomposing the tensor network into matrix products, this proposal shows that TMTP states can be efficiently represented as shallow quantum circuits consisting of approximately O(log^2 D) depth single-qubit gates, facilitating both quantum and classical computations.

The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations.

We investigate the possibility of formulating supergravity using a 1.5 ordered Lagrangian formalism and confirm that this approach cannot be accomplished. By applying a method developed by A.J. Singer, we prove that the 1.5 order formalism cannot generate a valid BRS transformation for a supergravity theory consisting of a metric field and a Majorana spinor field, given specific constraints: the theory must have three conformal symmetries, a Majorana spinor field with a standard kinetic term in the gravitational sector, and a non-zero coupling constant. These conditions are met by the Einstein-Cartan-Sciama-Kohnertan and Pure General Relativity theories when considered in conjunction with the Majorana gravitino field. However, our finding reveals that the 1.5 order formalism fails to validate v.Wieczorek's method for deriving a 1.5 ordered action associated with the Weyl multiplet in four-dimensional supergravity.

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to an external magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. We demonstrate that a 100-petawatt laser pulse passing through this type of plasma waveplate can be effectively converted from linear to circular polarization, maintaining full polarization transmission despite the immense 10^29 W/cm^2 intensity of the laser. The impact of this plasma waveplate is particularly pronounced when high-intensity lasers interact with solid targets, as it mitigates the rapid reflection caused by the generation of a high-magnetic-field target during this process.

Re-examining the search for a nonzero electric dipole moment (EDM) form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, in $\tau^+\tau^-$ production via $e^+e^-$ collisions between $\sqrt{s} = 10$ and $24$ GeV. An asymmetry in the $\tau$ and anti-$\tau$ production rates could indicate a non-zero value of $d_\tau(s)$. Using improved tau identification in the BESSIII detector, the $\tau^+\tau^-$ cross-section asymmetry is found to be consistent with zero at a confidence level of $I_{CL} \geq 0.15$ and $d_\tau$ constrained to a range based on form factor parameterizations, specifically $|d_\tau| < 1.44 \times 10^{-17} \, cm + 2.74 \times 10^{-18} \, cm \left(\frac{23.6 \, GeV}{\sqrt{s}}\right)^n$. With current and upcoming experiments in BESSIII and BESIII, more precise limits on $d_\tau$ can be set, with potential for improvements of up to $3\sigma$. Additionally, a shape asymmetry in the $\tau$ and anti-$\tau$ energy distributions provides another constraint on $d_\\tau$, resulting in $|d_\tau|

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of massless scalar field conformal block operators in AdS$_2$, in line with the non-trivial aspect of the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ holographic duality. Furthermore, this new perspective enables us to derive the weight-shifted conformal block expression for spinning primary fields as a natural extension of the well-established formula for scalar primary fields.

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance in preliminary trials. We take this by extending our model that incorporates both a precise foreground removal and solving for a gravitational lensing effect, to an upcoming experiment's configuration that mimics a signal similar to those that will be observed by next generation experiments, such as the Cosmic Microwave Background Intensity Map for Three-Dimensional Reconstruction of the Early Universe (CIMBAINE) and the Atacama Cosmic Microwave Background Explorers (ACAME-CR), respectively. We find that this neural network approach provides an accurate reconstruction of the distorted temperature perturbation power spectrum and a significant improvement in delensing precision, specifically by at least 10%, when compared to the standard approach.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio  an order of magnitude higher than the solar abundance ratio. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling place SN~2020jfo's mass in the range 12-16 solar masses.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses in a $\Lambda$CDM model. Results showed that including velocity information significantly improved prediction accuracy by a factor of 3 when comparing 2D mass estimates to mass estimates based on velocity and density alone, which is expected to IOP publications as it highlights the importance of velocity fields in the formation of dark matter halos. Furthermore, the model exhibited a tendency to predict lower masses for objects with similar velocity and density data, which is believed to be caused by differences in the cosmic velocity field and supports the hypothesis that velocity fields have a crucial role in the formation of dark matter halos.

Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both slow and fast rotation regimes, as well as during various phases of stellar evolution, in aligning with independent simulation results. This validates the method's effectiveness and potential for a broader understanding of evolving rotating stars.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves, which cannot be achieved with traditional parameter estimation methods due to their lengthy computation times. This paper introduces novel deep learning approaches, namely a sparse representation method and a sequence-to-sequence learning technique using a fully connected dictionary, which provide rapid and precise signal classification between neutron star mergers and binary black holes. The sequence-to-sequence technique also enables downstream prediction of frequency evolution in a 2D spectral density diagram, indicating its potential for signal classification and further studies. Novel losses are also proposed to enhance the performance of these methods, particularly the fully connected dictionary which demonstrates superior results compared to conventional neural network architectures in terms of area under the curve and runtime. Furthermore, this research presents an alternative approach employing a generative model called a score-based neural network, which also achieves accurate and rapid signal classification and exceeds the performance of comparable methods, including the fully connected dictionary, in terms of classification accuracy and processing time.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Center to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we term FNE-RS-TS. In this design, we transform long-text classification tasks into easier token-level tasks, effectively minimizing the negative effects of redundant or conflicting relationships.

To validate the effectiveness of our system, we conducted comprehensive experiments utilizing the N2C2 evaluation metrics. Results showed substantial improvements when using the FNE-RS-TS design compared to a baseline model. Moreover, our system demonstrated significant performance gains of approximately 10% to 20% across most social determinants when incorporating the proposed strategy, outperforming

This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with potential for short-term economic and social benefits turning into prolonged setbacks.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. These objects, whether formed through the accretion of matter or the merging of others, cease their growth within less than 100 orbits of the nearest parent star. As a result, they either accrete and break down again or merge with other disks, effectively preventing any "super-Angular Momentum Objects" from coming into existence. This phenomenon is attributed to the interaction between the star and its surrounding disk, wherein the star's angular momentum causes a breakdown in accretion streams due to shearing forces, thus maintaining a degree of uniformity in the mass of disk fragments.

Furthermore, evidence from these simulations indicates that episodic accretion streams and disk instabilities are not the primary causes of variability observed in these objects, as they occur on a timescale that is much shorter than those events. Instead, variability may stem from other sources, such as different modes of activity within the disk or the accretion stream, as they operate on a broader timescale.

Additionally, these simulations provide a potential source for fueling events in objects such as ultra-luminous X-ray binaries, Tauri variables, and luminous compact stellar nuclei, as the potential energy stored in these objects may be released in a more efficient and less erratic manner.

Overall, these findings provide a potential source for the observed phenomena mentioned above, as they are not

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that a given theory is completely characterized by its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix under specific conditions. By applying a procedure grounded in von Neumann algebras, we've derived multiple families of interacting wedge-local nets, one of which is closely related to Buchholz-Lechner-Summers' chiral CFT deformation. We've also successfully isolated the strictly local elements in another instance. Furthermore, using endomorphisms on the U(1)-current net and the free fermion net developed by Longo-Witten, we've constructed a large family of wedge-local nets.

Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower exposure among children and occupants of sensitive locations, including schools and medical facilities. To address these concerns, a systematic approach is outlined to numerically evaluate downlink 5G exposure among children, adolescents, schools, and medical centers, also applicable to pre-5G scenarios. This methodology is then applied to two real-world case studies. Findings indicate that as 5G adoption increases, so too will the exposure from 5G cellular towers. However, international safety guidelines still remain unaffected by these findings. Interestingly, children experiencing higher exposure levels than older individuals is attributed to their smaller stature, a key distinction between kids and adults, in effect reducing the elevation of 5G antennas relative to a child's head, thereby increasing the likelihood of direct exposure to 5G antennas. Furthermore, it is discovered that exposure levels from 5G towers are lower than their 4G/5G counterparts due to 5G's higher operating frequencies, which facilitate reduced transmission ranges, a benefit leveraging 5G's capability for highly localized and efficient signal delivery.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their intensity and direction. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model through direct numerical simulations and compared its results with those from fully nonlinear simulations, demonstrating accuracy across a broad spectrum of parameters.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully employed to achieve safe and efficient navigation. Notable findings indicate that multi-sonar detection allows for the identification of obstructed passages, resulting in enhanced navigational performance.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. We then propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for each user and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an efficient yet suboptimal solution strategy. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a relevant benchmark solution.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels.

Kopczyński and Waśkiewski enhanced traditional finite sup-torch games by incorporating a totally ordered group in the computation of supremal and infimal values, particularly within the domain of real numbers. This extension has significant relevance for analyzing differential equations and Dijkstra's testability. In this work, we generalize these ideas to any totally ordered group, combining this with recent discoveries about countable, supersolvable groups, and exploring their potential applications in parity and G-parity games.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we set up a fluid dynamics test case involving a periodic flow around a deformable structure, solving the problem both analytically and numerically.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

One of the key effects of quantum mechanics, which has significant societal implications, is that of atomic interference. To effectively measure local magnetic field changes with high sensitivity and high resolution, it's crucial to minimize random errors (noise) in the measurement of this effect. In this study, we introduce a novel, low-noise method for measuring the Meissner effect in atoms interferometry. By employing the superconducting expulsion of magnetic fields, we can effectively reduce the noise present in the measurement of local magnetic fields, as well as other quantities related to atomic properties. This enables us to achieve a noise level as low as 15 pT/$\sqrt{\mathrm{s}}$ in the measurement of local magnetic field changes using rubidium atoms.

We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature via Fermi statistics, we simulate this system and reveal substantial changes in spin-polarized entropy for energies beyond MoTe$_2$-EuO's bandgap.
